data.title: Turčianske Jaseno – Hradište, a promontory hillfort above the Vôdka valley
data.excerpt: A mountain promontory south-east of Turčianske Jaseno, known as Hradište, rises abruptly some 80 m above a flat saddle and is defended by three ramparts enclosing 5.2 hectares. Štefan Janšák, who published the site in 1930, found sherds of the Púchov culture here; Slavic pottery later placed Hradište among the potential Slavic hillforts.
data.metaTitle: Turčianske Jaseno – Hradište, a promontory hillfort
data.metaDescription: Hradište (spot height 696) south-east of Turčianske Jaseno rises some 80 m above a saddle. Three ramparts and Púchov-culture sherds mark the site.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Spot height 696 (Hradište) lies south-east of Turčianske Jaseno; the valley of the Vôdka brook runs to the south, and a ridge runs from Tlstý diel (862 m) towards Belá. Hradište rises some 80 m above a flat saddle east of Horné Jeseno.

keyFacts.label: Natural defences
keyFacts.value: Nature protected the hillfort on three sides — slopes falling at 35 to 45 degrees (the sides b – c – e and d – e – f); free, unhindered access was only from the south-west, in the zone b – a – i.

keyFacts.label: The three ramparts
keyFacts.value: Three ramparts: the clear rampart i – k – h, 112 m long, on the north; the levelled rampart g – j, now only a terrain swell 10 – 15 cm high; and the arched rampart d – 696 – f, 74 m long, 8 m high outwards and 6 m inwards.

keyFacts.label: Area of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: The hillfort had a total area of 5.2 ha: an outer enclosure of 5.04 ha and a level acropolis of 0.16 ha, on which the most important man of the hillfort is assumed to have resided.

keyFacts.label: Archaeological finds
keyFacts.value: On the acropolis and around the rampart i – h, Š. Janšák found both coarse-grained and fine-grained sherds, graphite-coated on the surface, belonging to the period of the Púchov culture.

keyFacts.label: A potential Slavic hillfort
keyFacts.value: The find of Slavic pottery led both Dr Šalkovský and Dr Hulínek to place the hillfort among the potential Slavic hillforts, the so-called “uncertain fortified hilltop settlements”.

keyFacts.label: The legend of the Destruction of Hradište
keyFacts.value: The website of the village of Turčianske Jaseno preserves a legend about the end of the hillfort, “Skaza Hradišťa” (The Destruction of Hradište), set at the beginning of the 10th century; it is a folk legend, not a verified historical fact.

keyFacts.label: First researcher
keyFacts.value: The hillfort was discovered and first published by Š. Janšák in 1930.

timeline.description: Slavic pottery has also been found at the hillfort, which led both Dr Šalkovský and Dr Hulínek to place it among the potential Slavic hillforts.

timeline.description: The hillfort was discovered and first published by Š. Janšák in 1930.

timeline.description: On the acropolis and around it Š. Janšák found sherds of the Púchov culture, which attested to occupation of the hillfort in that period.

children.text: Spot height 696, which lies south-east of the village of Turčianske Jaseno, bears the name Hradište. South of the hillfort lies the valley of the Vôdka brook. From the hill of Tlstý diel, spot height 862, a mountain ridge runs towards the village of Belá, interrupted east of the village of Horné Jeseno by a flat saddle. Hradište rises abruptly to a height of about 80 m above this saddle and then falls away into the valley of the Vôdka brook. In the direction of the main fall of the slope the mountain promontory ends in a gentle incline, and against the fall in a sharp tooth of rock, which was used to build the hillfort. The hillfort was discovered and first published by Š. Janšák in 1930.

The ground plan of the hillfort is given by an acute angle with the sides b c e and i k e and its apex at e. The side b c e is at the same time the edge along which the terrain breaks and falls at an angle of about 35 degrees. The same applies to the side i h e, in the stretch h e. The steepest slope is in the stretch d e f, where it falls at an angle of 45 degrees. On three sides, then, nature created a perfect defence. On the south-western side, in the zone b a i, access is free and unhindered.

blocks.caption: A sketch plan of the hillfort after Š. Janšák
blocks.alt: A sketch plan of the hillfort after Š. Janšák

children.text: The clearly visible rampart i k h, 112 m long, lies on the northern side, in the stretch where the natural step in the terrain is neither steep nor high enough. Next comes the levelled rampart g j, a second line of defence connected with the preceding one. It appears only as a swell in the terrain 10 – 15 cm high. And finally we find here the massive arched rampart d – 696 – f, 74 m long. At the points d f it joins the steep hillside and has no height at all. From there it rises as far as spot height 696. On the outside, towards the south-west, it is 8 m high; towards the interior of the summit plateau, towards the north-east, 6 m.

blocks.caption: The hillfort clearly marked on a map of the Second Military Survey from the 19th century
blocks.alt: The hillfort clearly marked on a map of the Second Military Survey from the 19th century

children.text: The area of the hillfort amounts to 5.2 ha (between the lines a b c e i a) and can be divided into two parts. The first, with an area of 5.04 ha (I), forms the outer enclosure, sloping gently from the highest summit 696 towards the south-west. It is very well suited for putting up dwellings and possibly for keeping herds, all the more so because it is protected against the northern winds by the summit d e f and by the artificial rampart. The second part (II), a completely level plateau d e f d with an area of 0.16 ha, forms the core, or acropolis, perfectly protected on all sides, on which the most important man of the hillfort evidently resided.

On the acropolis Š. Janšák found two sherds, and he found others north-west of the rampart i h, immediately below it and in the fields in its neighbourhood. The sherds are coarse-grained and poorly fired. Further sherds are fine-grained, graphite-coated on the break and especially on the surface. The finds belong to the period of the Púchov culture, in which the hillfort was already occupied.

children.text: Dr Šalkovský states that Slavic pottery has also been found at the hillfort, and for that reason he places it among the potential Slavic hillforts, using specifically the term “uncertain fortified hilltop settlements”. Dr Hulínek likewise places it among the potential Slavic hillforts. On the website of the village of Turčianske Jaseno you can find this splendid legend about the hillfort, set at the beginning of the 10th century:

blocks.text:
“Above Turčianske Jaseno rises the hill of Hradište. On its summit, 695 metres high, lie the remains of earthen ramparts. A few years ago a shaft was dug here. In it were found the remains of charred beams, witnesses to an ancient tragedy in the history of Turiec.

On one hot July day in the year of our Lord 907, near Bratislava “the glory of the Slavs went down”. “The heathen hordes came flooding in, they cut down the Slav host” – so the poet Juraj Zvestoň Bulla mourned the fate of the Slovak folk, of those heroes who were left slain in the Danubian land by the spears of Old Hungarian horsemen and the swords of Bavarian knights. Great Moravia was brought to its knees, and on the ruins of the Old Slavic dwellings rose the homes of new Hungarian local lords.

For a long time these new living spaces were enough for them; they had no wish to go up into the valleys among the mountains, where the dense forests threatened resistance from the local people. In the Slovak mountains the spirit of Great Moravia still lingered on in the fortlets and the hillforts.

Among the mightiest of them was Vyšehrad, towering between the Nitra region and Turiec. The chieftain Zvan had his seat there. The neighbouring fortlets were subject to his power, among them this one, which the elder Lysoň built for himself on a steep hill in the north-eastern corner of the Turiec Basin. It afforded fitting protection, for steep ground surrounded it on three sides and only the rise to its north offered freer entry.

Indeed there was need to think of defence. At the councils of the elders Zvan warned ever more often: – The enemy will not be satisfied until he has seized even the last remnants of our ancient glorious homeland. We must prepare for a hard fight. Let us at least keep that pride and courage which our forefathers instilled in us. Let us show our descendants that we shall not bow our heads before evil, that we shall not lay them down lightly under the enemy's sword!

Such a warning was not enough for Zvan, and he went on. – Yet in vain shall we stand in resistance if we do not go on holding together as one. For we know well how our realm of Great Moravia fell into the dust precisely because of the quarrels and disputes of the sons of the famous Svatopluk!

Such wise words fell also upon the receptive mind of the chieftain Lysoň. He had two sons – the elder Jasoň and the younger Klaboň. Yet despite their father's remonstrations and warnings the sons could not find a brotherly bond. Klaboň was capricious and discontented; something at his father's fortlet was always not enough for him. It galled him particularly that fate had assigned him the part of the younger heir, and so he hated his brother Jasoň with all his soul.

Nothing else remained for Lysoň but to build Klaboň a dwelling of his own. On a steep hill above the valley, where on one side Katova skala gleamed white out of the thicket of the forest, a new fortlet rose, and it seemed that the strife between the brothers had been averted for good… Yet the rulers from the Danube were given no peace by the outlines of the mountains darkening on the northern horizon. They were lured by the thought that their subjects were living up there after all, and that these must be shown who was master here now. Spies brought them word that the order of the former empire still held there, that its chieftains kept together as one and that their resistance would not easily be broken. Surely it would be best to digest such a morsel piece by piece, to break up their strength. And a way would be found; the best, probably, would be the one that made use of the greatest weakness of the Slavs, their bickering and intolerance.

One spring evening a strange wayfarer knocked at the gate of Klaboň's fortlet. He asked to speak with the lord; he was bringing him, he said, a message from Nitra…

Zvan at Vyšehrad surely knew by now that the time had come to prepare for defence. He ordered the elders to strengthen the watches at the fortlets that were their seats. If they sighted foreign men-at-arms, they were to light the woodpiles prepared in advance. The beacons and the smoke would announce where help was needed.

But a flood spreads not by one road but by many. And so one evening the watchmen at Jasoň's fortlet saw the fires of warning beacons flare up on the western horizon above Vyšehrad, and above Vtáčnik to the south, and even on nearby Dedošová. The new morning had not had time to break with dawn above Lysec and Jarabina when a troop of foreign horsemen appeared in the valley below the steep slope of the fortlet. They left their horses by the brook and began to scramble up the bluff.

The defenders stood all around the structure of the fortlet, leaving free only the way from the north, from which help was coming from Klaboň's fortlet. Already their garments gleamed white and their swords and axes flashed. But instead of hurling themselves upon the enemy, Klaboň's men set upon Jasoň's horrified warriors.

The traitor Klaboň pierced his brother's breast with his own hand. It was a mercy that their father, old Lysoň, did not live to see it.

- Now I shall be lord of two strongholds! – Klaboň declared before the commander of the enemy host. But the commander replied. – If you have betrayed your own brother, you may as easily betray the whole of our Hungarian homeland! – And Klaboň, in helpless despair, when he recognised his immense guilt, threw himself into the flames that had begun to ravage his native dwelling. On its site there later rose the walls of the new castle of Sklabiňa.”
blocks.source: Skaza Hradišťa — a legend from the website of the village of Turčianske Jaseno
